en.title: Actuarial Science: the whole course
en.short: What actuarial science covers, how the degree is organised, and how to study it.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text: These notes are for learning, not professional advice. Actuarial practice is regulated, and rules, exam syllabuses and professional standards change. They also differ between countries. Before you rely on a formula, a standard or a regulation, check the current official source: your professional body, your regulator, or your own course handbook.

sections.heading: What actuarial science is
sections.text:
Actuarial science uses mathematics, statistics, economics and finance to measure and manage future financial risk. An actuary puts a number on uncertain future events: how long people will live, how often cars will crash, how much a pension scheme must hold today to pay benefits decades from now.

The work has three parts. You build a model of the future. You choose assumptions, such as mortality or interest rates. You then estimate the money needed and explain the result to people who must decide. Communication matters as much as the mathematics.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. A bachelor’s degree commonly takes three or four years; in many Nigerian universities it is four. It may be called BSc Actuarial Science and sit in a mathematics, statistics or business school.

Early years build foundations in calculus, linear algebra, probability and statistics, with economics, accounting and computing. Later years cover life contingencies, general insurance, pensions and finance. Many programmes give exemptions from some professional examinations.

Professional bodies include the Institute and Faculty of Actuaries (IFoA) in the UK and the Society of Actuaries (SOA) in the US. Nigeria has the Nigerian Actuarial Society. A master’s degree adds advanced modelling, data science and a dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory stage: calculus and linear algebra, probability, statistical inference, financial mathematics, economics, accounting, business finance, computing, and an overview of actuarial science and risk.

Core stage: survival models and life contingencies, life insurance and annuities, reserves and policy values, multiple decrement and multi-state models, pensions, health insurance and long-term care. General insurance follows, with pricing and reserving. Then risk theory and credibility, stochastic processes, regression modelling, financial economics, derivatives and hedging, asset-liability management, simulation, and professional ethics.

Master’s stage: advanced life contingencies and stochastic mortality, enterprise risk management and solvency, actuarial data science and machine learning, and research methods with a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Actuarial science is learned by working problems, not by reading. After each idea, do a short calculation by hand and check every step. Keep a formula sheet in your own words, and note the assumptions each formula needs.

Learn the meaning before the algebra. Ask what a survival probability, a discount factor or a reserve represents in money and time. Then practise past examination questions under time pressure.

Work in small groups and explain a solution aloud. If you cannot explain it simply, you do not yet know it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students memorise formulas without knowing when they apply. A discount function, a force of interest and a rate of discount are different tools.

Other frequent errors:
Using the wrong time unit, so that months are mixed with years.
Forgetting that a life table and an interest rate must refer to the same basis.
Confusing a reserve with a premium, or a claim with an expense.
Treating one country’s regulation or tax rule as universal.
Rounding too early in a long calculation.
Presenting a number without saying what it means for the decision.

keyPoints: Actuarial science measures uncertain future cash flows and the money needed to meet them.
A degree builds mathematics and statistics first, then life and general insurance applications.
Degree length, awards and exemptions differ by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Professional bodies such as the IFoA and SOA set examinations; Nigeria has the Nigerian Actuarial Society.
Learn the meaning of each formula and its assumptions before memorising it.
Practise full calculations under time pressure and state what the answer means.

en.title: Calculus and Linear Algebra for Actuaries
en.short: Limits, derivatives, integrals, series, matrices and eigenvalues applied to interest, growth and risk.

sections.heading: Change and accumulation
sections.text: Calculus studies change. A limit is the value that a sequence or function approaches. The derivative measures the immediate rate of change: if A(t) is an amount growing with time, A'(t) is approximately [A(t + h) − A(t)] ÷ h for small h. The integral measures accumulated change: the integral from a to b of f(t) dt is the area under the curve, and the fundamental theorem says integration reverses differentiation. Actuaries use derivatives for marginal rates and integrals to add continuous payments or risk over time.

sections.heading: Series and interest
sections.text: A sequence is an ordered list; a series is its sum. The geometric series 1 + x + x² + ... equals 1 ÷ (1 − x) when |x| < 1. This underlies annuity factors. For interest, the limit of (1 + r ÷ n)^n as n grows without bound is e^r, where e ≈ 2.71828. So continuous compounding gives A = P e^{rt}, and its derivative is A'(t) = rA(t): growth is proportional to size. Check: P = 1000, r = 5% = 0.05, t = 2 years. A = 1000 × e^{0.10} = 1000 × 1.10517 = 1105.17. Annual compounding gives 1000 × 1.05² = 1102.50, so continuous compounding adds 2.67.

sections.heading: Matrices and eigenvalues
sections.text: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. Matrix multiplication combines rows and columns. A system of linear equations can be written Ax = b, where A holds coefficients, x the unknowns and b the constants. It has a unique solution when A is invertible. An eigenvalue λ and eigenvector v satisfy Av = λv; λ shows how a linear transformation stretches its eigenvector. In risk work, matrices can hold transition or covariance information, and eigenvalues help reveal dominant directions of variation.

keyPoints: A limit is the value a sequence or function approaches.
The derivative is a rate of change; the integral accumulates change and reverses differentiation.
The geometric series 1 + x + x² + ... equals 1 ÷ (1 − x) for |x| < 1.
Continuous compounding: A = P e^{rt}, and A'(t) = rA(t).
A linear system Ax = b has a unique solution when A is invertible.
An eigenvalue λ satisfies Av = λv for a nonzero eigenvector v.

en.title: Probability Foundations
en.short: Sample spaces, probability axioms, Bayes, random variables, distributions, moments, joint laws and CLT.

sections.heading: Sample spaces and axioms
sections.text: A sample space S lists all possible outcomes of an experiment; an event is a subset of S. Events are disjoint if they cannot happen together. Probability P assigns each event a number from 0 to 1. The axioms are: P(S)=1; P(A)≥0; and for disjoint events P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B). From these come P(not A)=1−P(A) and P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). When outcomes are equally likely, P(A)=number in A÷total number.

sections.heading: Conditioning and Bayes
sections.text: Conditional probability is P(A|B)=P(A∩B)÷P(B), for P(B)>0. Rearranging gives the multiplication rule P(A∩B)=P(A|B)P(B). Bayes theorem reverses a condition: P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)÷P(B). For a partition, P(B)=ΣP(B|A_i)P(A_i). It updates a prior probability P(A) into a posterior P(A|B). Example: P(A)=0.01, P(B|A)=0.9 and P(B|not A)=0.05. Then P(B)=0.9×0.01+0.05×0.99=0.0585, so P(A|B)=0.009÷0.0585≈0.154.

sections.heading: Random variables and moments
sections.text: A random variable maps outcomes to numbers. It is discrete if it takes countable values, with probability mass function p(x)=P(X=x), and continuous with density f(x). Common discrete laws: Bernoulli, binomial and Poisson. Common continuous laws: uniform, exponential and normal. Expectation is E(X)=Σx p(x) or ∫x f(x)dx. Variance is Var(X)=E[(X−μ)²]=E(X²)−μ², where μ=E(X). For Bernoulli(p), E(X)=p and Var(X)=p(1−p). For binomial(n,p), E(X)=np and Var(X)=np(1−p). Poisson(λ) has mean and variance λ. For a fair die, E(X)=21÷6=3.5 and Var(X)=91÷6−3.5²=35÷12≈2.92.

sections.heading: Joint laws and CLT
sections.text: For two variables, the joint distribution gives P(X=x,Y=y) or a joint density. Marginal distributions come from summing or integrating out the other variable. X and Y are independent if P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)P(Y=y); then E(XY)=E(X)E(Y). Covariance is Cov(X,Y)=E(XY)−E(X)E(Y). Correlation is Cov(X,Y)÷√[Var(X)Var(Y)]. The central limit theorem says that, under finite variance, the sum or mean of many independent observations is approximately normal for large samples. For independent X_i with mean μ and variance σ², the sample mean has mean μ and variance σ²÷n. This explains why the normal law is common.

keyPoints: Probability axioms give P(S)=1, P(A)≥0 and P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B) for disjoint events.
Conditional probability is P(A|B)=P(A∩B)÷P(B), and Bayes theorem is P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)÷P(B).
Expectation is E(X)=Σx p(x) or ∫x f(x)dx, and variance is Var(X)=E(X²)−[E(X)]².
Bernoulli(p) has mean p and variance p(1−p); binomial(n,p) has mean np and variance np(1−p).
Independence means P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)P(Y=y), and then Cov(X,Y)=0.
The central limit theorem makes sums and means of many independent observations approximately normal for large samples.

en.title: Statistical Inference and Estimation
en.short: Sampling distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, chi-square and t tests, and simple regression.

sections.heading: Sampling and estimation
sections.text:
A statistic such as a sample mean varies between samples. Its sampling distribution is the distribution of the statistic over repeated samples of the same size. The standard error (SE) is its standard deviation; for a mean, SE = s ÷ √n, where s is the sample standard deviation and n the sample size. The central limit theorem says that for large n the sample mean is approximately Normal if observations are independent.

A point estimate is one number, such as xbar for the population mean mu. A 95% confidence interval is xbar ± t × SE, with t from the t distribution and n − 1 degrees of freedom. Example: n = 25, xbar = 10, s = 2. SE = 2 ÷ √25 = 0.4. With df = 24, t = 2.064. Interval = 10 ± 2.064 × 0.4 = 10 ± 0.826, or (9.174, 10.826).

sections.heading: Hypothesis tests
sections.text:
A hypothesis test compares a null hypothesis H0 with an alternative H1. Choose a significance level alpha, often 0.05. The p-value is the probability, if H0 is true, of a result at least as extreme as observed. Reject H0 if p < alpha.

For a mean, t = (xbar − mu0) ÷ (s ÷ √n). In the example, test H0: mu = 9. Then t = (10 − 9) ÷ 0.4 = 2.5. With df = 24, the two-sided p-value is about 0.02, so reject H0 at 5%.

sections.heading: Chi-square and regression
sections.text:
A chi-square test compares observed counts O with expected counts E: chi-square = Σ((O − E)² ÷ E). It tests goodness of fit or association in contingency tables.

A t test compares means; two-sample and paired versions are common. Simple linear regression models y = a + bx. Least squares chooses a and b to minimise Σ(y − a − bx)². The slope is b = Σ((x − xbar)(y − ybar)) ÷ Σ(x − xbar)². Check independence, linearity and constant variance.

keyPoints: The sampling distribution describes how a statistic varies over repeated samples, and its standard deviation is the standard error.
For a sample mean, SE = s ÷ √n, and a 95% confidence interval is xbar ± t × SE with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
A hypothesis test compares H0 with H1; reject H0 when the p-value is below the chosen significance level alpha.
For a mean, t = (xbar − mu0) ÷ (s ÷ √n); the t test is common for one-sample, two-sample and paired means.
The chi-square statistic is chi-square = Σ((O − E)² ÷ E), used for goodness of fit and association in contingency tables.
In simple linear regression y = a + bx, least squares gives slope b = Σ((x − xbar)(y − ybar)) ÷ Σ(x − xbar)².

en.title: Financial Mathematics: Interest and Annuities
en.short: Accumulation, discounting, annuities, equations of value, loans, NPV and IRR.

sections.heading: Accumulation and discounting
sections.text: Accumulation moves money forward in time; discounting moves it back. With simple interest, interest is paid only on the original principal: A = P(1 + i t), where i is the rate per period and t the number of periods. With compound interest, interest earns interest: A = P(1 + i)^n. The discount factor is v = 1 ÷ (1 + i), so a future amount A has present value PV = A v^n. The effective annual rate expresses a year’s growth as one rate.

sections.heading: Annuities certain
sections.text: An annuity certain is a series of fixed payments for a fixed term, with no dependence on survival. An annuity immediate pays at each period end. Its present value is a_n = (1 − v^n) ÷ i, and its accumulation is s_n = ((1 + i)^n − 1) ÷ i. An annuity due pays at each period start, so multiply these by (1 + i).

sections.heading: Equations of value and loans
sections.text: An equation of value compares cash flows at one common date. For a loan, the outstanding balance rolls forward with interest and falls by each payment: balance after payment = previous balance × (1 + i) − payment. Example: a 1,000 loan at 10% grows to 1,100 after one year; a payment of 400 leaves 700. A loan schedule lists interest, payment, principal repaid and balance each period.

sections.heading: NPV and IRR
sections.text: Net present value (NPV) discounts all cash flows at a required rate: NPV = Σ C_t v^t. Accept a project if NPV is positive. The internal rate of return (IRR) is the rate where NPV = 0. Example: pay 1,000 now and receive 600 after one and two years at 10%. NPV = −1,000 + 600 ÷ 1.1 + 600 ÷ 1.1² = 41.32. The IRR solves 1,000 = 600 ÷ (1 + r) + 600 ÷ (1 + r)², giving r ≈ 13.07%.

keyPoints: Simple interest uses A = P(1 + i t); compound interest uses A = P(1 + i)^n.
The discount factor is v = 1 ÷ (1 + i), so PV = A v^n.
For an annuity immediate, a_n = (1 − v^n) ÷ i and s_n = ((1 + i)^n − 1) ÷ i; multiply by (1 + i) for an annuity due.
An equation of value compares cash flows at one date, and a loan balance is previous balance × (1 + i) − payment.
NPV = Σ C_t v^t; a positive NPV means the project adds value at the required rate.
The IRR is the rate where NPV = 0, and it is compared with the required return.

en.title: Economics for Actuaries: Markets, Macro and Risk
en.short: Demand, supply, market structure, inflation, interest rates, unemployment and business cycles in insurance and pensions.

sections.heading: Demand, supply, markets
sections.text: Demand is the quantity of a good or service buyers want at each price. Supply is the quantity sellers offer. The demand curve usually slopes downward: at lower prices, buyers want more. The supply curve usually slopes upward: at higher prices, sellers offer more. Where they meet is the equilibrium price and quantity. Elasticity measures how much quantity responds to a price change. Market structure describes competition. Perfect competition has many small firms and identical products. Monopoly has one seller. Oligopoly has a few large sellers. Monopolistic competition has many sellers with differentiated products. Insurers operate in markets that are often oligopolistic or monopolistically competitive, and regulation matters.

sections.heading: Macroeconomic forces
sections.text: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. It reduces the buying power of money. Interest rates are the cost of borrowing and the return on saving. Central banks often raise rates to control inflation. Unemployment is when people who are seeking work cannot find jobs; the unemployment rate is the share of the labour force without work. The business cycle is the pattern of expansion and contraction in economic activity. During a boom, output and employment rise. In a recession, they fall. These forces interact and affect households and firms.

sections.heading: Effects on insurance
sections.text: Insurance and pensions are long-term promises, so macro forces matter. Inflation raises claim costs and erodes the real value of fixed pensions. Interest rates affect the present value of future payments, what future money is worth today, and the price of annuities. Higher rates lower present values. Unemployment and recessions can reduce premium income, increase some claims and lower investment returns. Pensions face contribution gaps and funding strain when asset values fall. A simple check: a fixed pension of ₦500,000 a year loses buying power when prices rise. At 20% inflation, its real value after one year is 500,000 ÷ 1.20 = ₦416,667. Actuaries must allow for these economic effects in pricing, reserving and funding.

keyPoints: Demand slopes downward and supply slopes upward; equilibrium sets price and quantity.
Market structure ranges from perfect competition to monopoly, with oligopoly and monopolistic competition between.
Inflation erodes real values; after one year, real value = nominal amount ÷ (1 + inflation).
Interest rates change the present value of future insurance and pension payments.
Unemployment and business cycles affect claims, premiums and investment returns.
Actuaries must reflect these economic forces in pricing, reserving and funding.

en.title: Accounting and Financial Statements for Actuaries
en.short: The three main statements, ratio analysis, and basic valuation and reporting ideas.

sections.heading: The three statements
sections.text:
The balance sheet, often called the statement of financial position, lists assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time. The accounting equation is Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Assets are resources controlled by the firm; liabilities are obligations; equity is the owners’ residual interest.

The income statement reports revenue and expenses over a period and gives profit. It usually uses accrual accounting, so revenue is recorded when earned, not when cash arrives. The cash flow statement explains the change in cash under operating, investing and financing activities. Profit and cash are not the same.

sections.heading: Ratio analysis
sections.text:
Ratios compare figures from the statements. Liquidity ratios include the current ratio (current assets ÷ current liabilities) and the quick ratio (current assets less inventory, divided by current liabilities). Profitability ratios include net margin (net profit ÷ revenue). Gearing compares debt with capital.

Example for a made-up firm:
current assets 300, inventory 100, current liabilities 150, revenue 800, net profit 80, equity 400, long-term debt 200.
Current ratio = 300 ÷ 150 = 2.0.
Quick ratio = (300 − 100) ÷ 150 = 1.33.
Net margin = 80 ÷ 800 = 10%.
Gearing = 200 ÷ (400 + 200) = 33.3%.

Ratios need context: compare with past years, competitors and industry. Definitions vary, so state the formula used.

sections.heading: Valuation and reporting
sections.text:
Financial reporting follows standards that differ by country. Many countries use IFRS, while the United States uses US GAAP. Standards aim to make statements comparable, but estimates and accounting policy choices remain.

Valuation estimates what an asset, liability or business is worth. Common bases are historical cost, fair value (the price to sell an asset or transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants) and present value of expected future cash flows. An actuary often adjusts accounting figures for risk and time.

Simple example: a business is expected to produce 100 each year forever and the required return is 10%. Value = 100 ÷ 0.10 = 1,000. Real valuations need growth and risk assumptions checked.

keyPoints: Assets = Liabilities + Equity.
The income statement measures profit over a period, while the cash flow statement explains the change in cash.
Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities; quick ratio = (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities.
Net margin = net profit ÷ revenue, and gearing compares debt with capital.
Ratios need comparison with past years, competitors and industry before they mean much.
Valuation can use historical cost, fair value or present value of future cash flows; reporting standards differ by country, with IFRS common and US GAAP used in the United States.

en.title: Business Finance and Capital Budgeting
en.short: Sources of finance, capital budgeting, cost of capital, working capital and firm decisions.

sections.heading: Sources of finance
sections.text: A firm raises money from equity or debt. Equity means selling shares; holders own part of the firm and receive dividends, which are not compulsory. Debt means borrowing; interest and repayment are contractual. Short-term sources include trade credit and bank overdrafts. Long-term sources include retained earnings, share issues, bonds and term loans. Leasing is another option. The choice affects control, risk and cost.

sections.heading: Capital budgeting
sections.text:
Capital budgeting is choosing long-term projects. It compares cash outflows now with future cash inflows. Net present value (NPV) discounts all cash flows at the cost of capital: NPV = Σ Ct ÷ (1 + r)^t − initial cost. Accept a project if NPV is positive. Payback is the time to recover the initial cost. Internal rate of return (IRR) is the discount rate that makes NPV zero.

Example: a machine costs 100,000 and returns 60,000 at the end of each of two years. At r = 10%, NPV = 60,000 ÷ 1.10 + 60,000 ÷ 1.21 − 100,000 = 54,545 + 49,587 − 100,000 = 4,132. Positive, so accept.

sections.heading: Cost of capital
sections.text: Cost of capital is the return investors require. It is the discount rate for projects of similar risk. Weighted average cost of capital (WACC) = (E ÷ V) × Ke + (D ÷ V) × Kd × (1 − T), where E is equity, D is debt, V = E + D, Ke is cost of equity, Kd is cost of debt and T is the tax rate. Debt is cheaper partly because interest is tax-deductible in many countries; check local tax rules. Higher debt raises financial risk.

sections.heading: Working capital and decisions
sections.text: Working capital = current assets − current liabilities. It measures short-term liquidity. Managers balance cash, inventory and receivables against payables. Too little risks insolvency; too much ties up funds. The financial decisions of a firm are investment, financing and dividend decisions. They interact: a project needs finance, finance has a cost, and dividends affect retained cash.

keyPoints: NPV = Σ Ct ÷ (1 + r)^t − initial cost; accept projects with positive NPV.
Payback is the time to recover the initial cost, but it ignores later cash flows and the time value of money.
WACC = (E ÷ V) × Ke + (D ÷ V) × Kd × (1 − T) is the discount rate for projects of similar risk.
Working capital = current assets − current liabilities.
Debt is cheaper than equity before tax but raises financial risk.
The three financial decisions are investment, financing and dividend decisions.

en.title: Computing and Data Analysis for Actuaries
en.short: Spreadsheets and R or Python for cleaning data, describing it, simple simulation and clear reporting.

sections.heading: Tools and workflow
sections.text: Actuaries use spreadsheets for quick checks and a statistical programming language such as R or Python for repeatable work. A spreadsheet stores data in cells and calculates with formulas. A script is a saved list of commands that can be rerun. Keep raw data unchanged, work on a copy, and record each step. This makes results reproducible: another person can repeat them and get the same answer.

sections.heading: Cleaning data
sections.text: Data cleaning means finding and fixing errors before analysis. Check for duplicate rows, missing values, inconsistent units and dates, and impossible entries such as a negative claim amount. Decide and record a rule for each problem: remove, correct or leave as missing. In a spreadsheet use sort, filter and lookup functions. In R or Python use table functions and logical tests. Never delete a value without a reason.

sections.heading: Describing data
sections.text:
Descriptive statistics summarise a dataset. The mean is the sum divided by the count. The median is the middle value when sorted. The standard deviation measures spread around the mean. For five claim amounts in thousands of naira, 120, 150, 180, 210 and 240:
mean = 900 ÷ 5 = 180
median = 180
deviations = −60, −30, 0, 30, 60
sum of squared deviations = 9,000
population variance = 9,000 ÷ 5 = 1,800
population standard deviation = √1,800 = 42.43
sample standard deviation = √(9,000 ÷ 4) = 47.43
State which you use. Spreadsheets and R or Python give both.

sections.heading: Simulation and presentation
sections.text: Simple simulation uses random numbers to study a calculation many times. In a spreadsheet, RAND() gives a random number between 0 and 1. In R or Python, set a seed so the run can be repeated. Run the model many times, then summarise the output with mean, median and range. Present results clearly: give units, round sensibly, label axes, and use a table or chart that answers the question. Do not hide uncertainty.

keyPoints: Keep raw data unchanged and record every cleaning step so work is reproducible.
The mean is the sum divided by the count; the median is the middle sorted value.
Population standard deviation = √(Σ(x − mean)² ÷ n); sample standard deviation divides by n − 1.
Use a spreadsheet for quick checks and a script in R or Python for repeatable analysis.
Simple simulation repeats a calculation with random inputs; set a seed so it can be rerun.
Present numbers with units, sensible rounding and clear labels.

en.title: Introduction to Actuarial Science and Risk
en.short: What actuaries do, how risk is managed, and the professional standards they follow.

sections.heading: What actuaries do
sections.text: Actuarial science applies mathematics, statistics and finance to uncertain future events, mainly to price and manage financial risk. In life insurance, actuaries estimate how long people may live and set premiums and reserves. In general insurance, they price risks such as fire or motor claims. In pensions, they estimate future benefit costs and funding. Wider fields include health, banking, investments, regulation and data analysis. They do not remove risk; they measure it and help organisations plan for it.

sections.heading: Risk management process
sections.text: Risk is the chance of loss or of results different from expectation. Risk management is the process of identifying, assessing, treating and monitoring risks. Identify: list exposures. Assess: estimate likelihood and impact. Treat: avoid, reduce, transfer by insurance, or accept. Monitor: review and update. A concrete case: a Lagos bus company owns 20 buses. It estimates a 2% chance per bus per year of a fire damaging a bus, with repair cost ₦1,500,000. Expected annual fire cost = 20 × 0.02 × 1,500,000 = ₦600,000. It may buy insurance, improve maintenance, or keep a reserve.

sections.heading: Professional bodies
sections.text: Actuaries belong to professional bodies that set education and practice standards. The International Actuarial Association (IAA) links national associations. Examples include the Institute and Faculty of Actuaries (IFoA) in the UK, the Society of Actuaries (SOA) and Casualty Actuarial Society (CAS) in the US, the Actuarial Society of South Africa (ASSA), and the Nigerian Actuarial Society. Qualifications and rules differ by country, so check the body for where you plan to work.

sections.heading: Code of conduct
sections.text: A code of conduct states the behaviour expected of members. Common principles are integrity, competence, objectivity, confidentiality and professional behaviour. Actuaries must keep skills current, use reliable data, explain assumptions honestly, and disclose conflicts of interest. Breaches can lead to discipline. The code protects the public and the profession’s reputation.

keyPoints: Actuarial science uses mathematics, statistics and finance to measure uncertain future financial events.
The risk management process is identify, assess, treat and monitor.
Expected annual cost = number of exposures × probability of loss × cost per loss.
Professional bodies set education and practice standards, and qualifications differ by country.
A code of conduct requires integrity, competence, objectivity, confidentiality and professional behaviour.
Actuaries work in insurance, pensions, health, investments, regulation and wider risk fields.

en.title: Life Contingencies: Survival Models
en.short: Future lifetime, survival functions, force of mortality, life tables and select mortality.

sections.heading: Future lifetime
sections.text: For a life aged x, the future lifetime random variable T_x is the remaining time until death. It is continuous. The complete lifetime is x + T_x. The curtate future lifetime is K_x = floor(T_x), the whole future years lived. The survival function is S_x(t) = P(T_x > t) = l_{x+t}/l_x in a life table. Its density is f_x(t) = −d/dt S_x(t).

sections.heading: Force and rates
sections.text: The force of mortality is μ_{x+t} = −(d/dt) ln S_x(t) = f_x(t)/S_x(t). It is an instantaneous death rate, not a probability. For small h, P(T_x ≤ h) ≈ h μ_x. The one-year death probability is q_x = 1 − p_x, where p_x = P(T_x > 1). In a life table, p_x = l_{x+1}/l_x and q_x = d_x/l_x. The complete expectation is E[T_x] = ∫_0^∞ S_x(t) dt; the curtate expectation is e_x = E[K_x] = Σ_{k≥1} k p_x.

sections.heading: Life table arithmetic
sections.text: Life tables list l_x, the number alive at exact age x, often from a radix such as 100,000. Then d_x = l_x − l_{x+1}. Example: l_40 = 90,000, l_41 = 89,100, l_42 = 88,050. Then d_40 = 900, q_40 = 900 ÷ 90,000 = 0.01, p_40 = 0.99. Also 2p_40 = l_42/l_40 = 88,050 ÷ 90,000 = 0.9783. The first two terms of e_40 are p_40 + 2p_40 = 0.99 + 0.9783 = 1.9683; later terms need more table entries.

sections.heading: Select mortality
sections.text: Select mortality means recent medical selection lowers mortality for a few years after entry. Actuaries write q_{[x]+r} for a life selected at age x and now aged x+r. During a select period of s years, q_{[x]+r} is usually lower than q_{x+r}; after s years the life is ultimate and q_{[x]+s} = q_{x+s}. Select tables need age at selection and duration.

keyPoints: T_x is the future lifetime; K_x = floor(T_x) is the curtate lifetime.
S_x(t) = P(T_x > t) = l_{x+t}/l_x.
μ_{x+t} = −(d/dt) ln S_x(t) = f_x(t)/S_x(t).
p_x = l_{x+1}/l_x and q_x = 1 − p_x = d_x/l_x.
e_x = E[K_x] = Σ_{k≥1} k p_x.
Select mortality q_{[x]+r} applies during the select period; ultimate rates apply afterwards.

en.title: Life insurance and life annuities: present values and premiums
en.short: Present values of life benefits and annuities, net premiums and gross premiums with expenses.

sections.heading: Present values
sections.text:
Whole life insurance pays a sum when the insured dies. Term insurance pays only if death occurs within n years. Endowment insurance pays on death within n years or on survival to n. In a discrete model the benefit is paid at the end of the year of death. With interest i, v = 1 ÷ (1 + i), and k p_x is the chance of surviving k years from age x. For a unit sum, the expected present value (EPV) of whole life is A_x = Σ v^(k+1) k p_x q_(x+k), over all k. Term is A^1_(x:n) = Σ v^(k+1) k p_x q_(x+k), for k = 0 to n−1. Endowment is A_(x:n) = A^1_(x:n) + v^n n p_x.

A life annuity due pays at the start of each year while alive: ä_x = Σ v^k k p_x, over all k. A temporary annuity due is ä_(x:n) = Σ v^k k p_x, for k = 0 to n−1.

sections.heading: Net and gross premiums
sections.text:
The equivalence principle sets the EPV of premiums equal to the EPV of benefits. For annual premiums P on whole life, P = A_x ÷ ä_x. For other benefits, use their EPV and the premium annuity factor. Net premiums ignore expenses.

Gross premiums include them: EPV of gross premiums = EPV of benefits + EPV of expenses. Expenses may be initial, renewal or claim costs; a percentage of premium is an expense loading.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
A two-year term policy pays 100,000 at the end of the year of death. q_x = 0.01, q_(x+1) = 0.02, i = 5%. EPV benefit = 100,000(0.952381 × 0.01 + 0.907029 × 0.99 × 0.02) = 2,748.30.

Premiums are payable at the start of each year while alive, so the annuity factor is 1 + 0.952381 × 0.99 = 1.942857. Net premium = 2,748.30 ÷ 1.942857 = 1,414.57. Add an initial expense of 100: gross premium = (2,748.30 + 100) ÷ 1.942857 = 1,466.04.

keyPoints: Whole life EPV: A_x = Σ v^(k+1) k p_x q_(x+k), with the sum over all k.
Term EPV: A^1_(x:n) = Σ v^(k+1) k p_x q_(x+k), for k = 0 to n−1.
Endowment EPV: A_(x:n) = A^1_(x:n) + v^n n p_x.
Annuity due EPV: ä_x = Σ v^k k p_x; temporary: ä_(x:n) = Σ v^k k p_x for k = 0 to n−1.
Net premium by equivalence: P = EPV benefits ÷ EPV premium annuity.
Gross premium: EPV gross premiums = EPV benefits + EPV expenses.

en.title: Reserves and Policy Values
en.short: Covers prospective and retrospective reserves, recursion, profit testing, and expenses and bonuses.

sections.heading: Two reserve views
sections.text: A policy value, or reserve, is the amount an insurer should hold for a policy. The prospective reserve is the expected present value (EPV) of future benefits and expenses minus the EPV of future premiums. The net premium reserve ignores expenses and uses net premiums; the gross premium reserve includes expenses and uses gross premiums. The retrospective reserve accumulates past premiums less past benefits and expenses, allowing for interest and survival. With the same assumptions and the same premium, the two views agree at any duration.

sections.heading: Recursion and example
sections.text:
For a unit benefit payable at the end of the year of death, the recursive reserve equation is (V_t + P)(1+i) = q_{x+t} + p_{x+t} V_{t+1}. Here V_t is the reserve just before the premium at time t, P is the premium, i the interest rate, and q and p are death and survival probabilities. It says the reserve plus premium, accumulated one year, meets the expected death claim plus the reserve needed if the life survives.

Example: sum assured 1,000, q_x=0.01, q_{x+1}=0.02, i=5%. EPV benefits = 1,000(0.01÷1.05 + 0.99×0.02÷1.05²)=27.48. Annuity due = 1 + 0.99÷1.05 = 1.9429. Net premium = 27.48÷1.9429 = 14.146. Prospective V_1 = 1,000×0.02÷1.05 − 14.146 = 4.902. Check recursion: (0 + 14.146)×1.05 = 0.01×1,000 + 0.99×4.902 = 14.853.

sections.heading: Profit testing and bonuses
sections.text: A profit test projects premiums, claims, expenses, interest and reserves year by year. An increase in reserve is a cash outflow; a release is an inflow. The profit vector is discounted at a risk discount rate to give a net present value (NPV), and the internal rate of return is compared with the required return. Expenses are split into initial, renewal and termination costs and are loaded into gross premiums. For participating policies, bonuses increase benefits and reserves; the actuary must allow for bonus loadings, declared bonus rates and terminal bonuses, and test whether the premium is sufficient.

keyPoints: Prospective reserve = EPV future benefits and expenses − EPV future premiums.
Retrospective reserve = accumulated past premiums − accumulated past benefits and expenses, allowing for survival.
Recursive reserve: (V_t + P)(1+i) = q_{x+t}S + p_{x+t}V_{t+1} for sum assured S.
Net premium reserves ignore expenses; gross premium reserves include them.
Profit testing discounts annual cash flows, including reserve increases, at a risk discount rate to get NPV.
Bonuses raise future benefits and reserves, so participating premiums need bonus loadings and testing.

en.title: Multiple Decrement and Multi-State Models
en.short: Competing risks, multiple and associated single decrement tables, and Markov multi-state models.

sections.heading: Competing risks
sections.text: A competing risk is a cause that removes a person from a state, such as death, sickness or retirement. When several causes act together, observing one prevents us from seeing the others. A multiple decrement table records, for each age, the number starting the year, exits by each cause, and the probability of exit from each cause in the presence of all causes. Write q_x^(j) for exit due to cause j and q_x^(τ) for exit from any cause. The associated single decrement table gives q_x'^(j), the probability if cause j acted alone. It helps compare causes and understand the multiple table.

sections.heading: Tables and example
sections.text: In a multiple decrement table the cause probabilities add: q_x^(τ) = Σ_j q_x^(j). Suppose 10,000 people aged 60 start a year. The table gives q^(death)=0.035, q^(disability)=0.050 and q^(retirement)=0.100. Then q^(τ)=0.185. Expected deaths = 10,000 × 0.035 = 350. Expected disability exits = 10,000 × 0.050 = 500. Expected retirements = 10,000 × 0.100 = 1,000. Expected survivors = 10,000 − 350 − 500 − 1,000 = 8,150. Check: 8,150 ÷ 10,000 = 0.815 = 1 − 0.185. Associated single decrement probabilities are hypothetical and do not simply add.

sections.heading: Multi-state models
sections.text: A multi-state model follows movement among states such as healthy, sick, disabled and dead. A Markov model assumes the next state depends only on the current state, not the path taken. Annual transition probabilities form a matrix P whose rows sum to 1. For states H (healthy), D (disabled) and X (dead), let P have rows: H to H 0.90, H to D 0.08, H to X 0.02; D to H 0.10, D to D 0.75, D to X 0.15; X to X 1. The two-year H to X probability is the H-X entry of P²: 0.90×0.02 + 0.08×0.15 + 0.02×1 = 0.050. The H to D entry is 0.90×0.08 + 0.08×0.75 = 0.132. The H to H entry is 0.90×0.90 + 0.08×0.10 = 0.818. These sum to 1.000.

keyPoints: A competing risk is a cause of exit that acts alongside other causes.
In a multiple decrement table q_x^(τ) = Σ_j q_x^(j) and p_x^(τ) = 1 − q_x^(τ).
An associated single decrement probability q_x'^(j) is the probability from cause j if it acted alone, and it is not generally equal to q_x^(j).
Under independent causes, survival from all causes is the product of the associated single decrement survival probabilities: p_x^(τ) = ∏_j (1 − q_x'^(j)).
A Markov multi-state model uses transition probabilities that depend only on the current state; each row of P sums to 1.
Two-year transition probabilities are entries of P², found by matrix multiplication.

en.title: Pension Schemes and Retirement Benefits
en.short: Defined benefit and defined contribution pensions, funding, valuation assumptions and regulation.

sections.heading: Two scheme types
sections.text: A defined benefit (DB) scheme promises a pension linked to salary and service. The employer or scheme bears the investment and longevity risk. A defined contribution (DC) scheme credits contributions to an individual account; the member bears investment risk and uses the fund to buy an annuity or draw income. Hybrid schemes mix features. Benefits may include a lump sum, spouse’s pension and indexation, but rules differ by country and scheme.

sections.heading: Funding and assumptions
sections.text: Pay-as-you-go funding meets pensions from current contributions or taxes; advance funding builds assets in advance. Actuaries use methods such as projected unit credit, entry age normal and aggregate funding to spread cost. Valuation assumptions include discount rate, salary growth, inflation, mortality, retirement age and withdrawal. A higher discount rate lowers the present value of liabilities. The funding ratio is assets ÷ liabilities. Assumptions must be disclosed and reviewed.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A DB scheme uses an accrual rate of 1/60 for each year of service. A member retires after 30 years on a pensionable salary of 120,000. Annual pension = (1/60) × 30 × 120,000 = 60,000. If the scheme holds assets of 900,000 and the actuarial liability is 1,000,000, the funding ratio = 900,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 90%, a deficit of 100,000. For a DC member, an opening fund of 500,000 grows at 5% a year for 10 years with no charges. Accumulated fund = 500,000 × 1.05^10 = 814,447, to the nearest unit. Check: 1.05^10 = 1.6288946, so 500,000 × 1.6288946 = 814,447.3.

sections.heading: Regulation and benefits
sections.text: Regulation sets funding rules, solvency margins, disclosure, tax treatment, portability and pension ages. Some countries require DB deficits to be funded within a set period; others rely more on pay-as-you-go. A pension regulator may supervise schemes and protect members. Because rules vary by country and change over time, check the current official source, such as the regulator or tax authority. Retirement benefits are not uniform across countries.

keyPoints: A DB scheme promises a pension based on salary and service, while a DC scheme provides a fund whose value depends on contributions and investment returns.
DB pension = accrual rate × years of service × pensionable salary.
DC accumulated fund = opening fund × (1 + return)^years, if there are no further contributions or charges.
Funding ratio = scheme assets ÷ actuarial liabilities; below 100% means a deficit.
Valuation assumptions such as discount rate, salary growth, mortality and retirement age change the measured liabilities.
Pension regulation, tax and benefit rules vary by country, so check the current official source.

en.title: Health Insurance and Long-Term Care
en.short: Morbidity, claim costs, premiums, reserves, risk sharing and regulation in health and LTC insurance.

sections.heading: Morbidity and claim costs
sections.text: Health insurance pays for medical treatment. Long-term care (LTC) insurance pays for help with daily living when illness or disability lasts a long time. Morbidity is the incidence, duration and severity of illness or disability. Claim cost is the amount paid per claim. Expected claim cost per member equals the probability of a claim multiplied by the average cost of a claim. For health cover, cost also depends on treatment prices, use of services and cost sharing. For LTC, duration is central: a small chance of a long stay can cost more than many short claims. Insurers use morbidity tables, claims data and country-specific medical inflation. Data quality varies, so assumptions must be checked.

sections.heading: Premiums and reserves
sections.text: Expected claims per member = probability of claim × average claim cost. A gross premium must also cover expenses, risk margin and profit. If expenses are a percentage e of the gross premium P, then P = (expected claims + risk margin + profit) ÷ (1 − e). Example: 10,000 members, claim probability 4%, average claim 150,000, profit set to zero. Expected claims = 0.04 × 150,000 = 6,000 per member. Risk margin = 5% × 6,000 = 300. Expenses = 15% of premium. P = (6,000 + 300) ÷ 0.85 = 7,411.76. Check: 0.15 × 7,411.76 = 1,111.76, and 6,000 + 300 + 1,111.76 = 7,411.76. A reserve is the present value of future benefits and expenses minus the present value of future premiums. For LTC, project transitions between healthy, disabled and dead.

sections.heading: Risk sharing and regulation
sections.text: Risk sharing reduces moral hazard and adverse selection. Tools include deductibles, co-payments, coinsurance, waiting periods, exclusions, provider networks and reinsurance. Rating may be community rated, with one rate for a whole pool, or experience rated, based on group claims. Regulation varies by country. Common issues are solvency capital, reserve standards, premium approval, mandated benefits, guaranteed renewability, consumer disclosure and treatment of pre-existing conditions. In Nigeria, the National Health Insurance Authority oversees health insurance; the United Kingdom mainly funds health care through taxation. Rules change, so check the current regulator and law.

keyPoints: Morbidity covers the incidence, duration and severity of illness or disability, and claim cost is the amount paid per claim.
Expected claim cost per member = probability of claim × average claim cost.
If expenses are a percentage e of gross premium P, P = (expected claims + risk margin + profit) ÷ (1 − e).
A reserve is the present value of future benefits and expenses minus the present value of future premiums.
Risk sharing tools include deductibles, co-payments, coinsurance, waiting periods, exclusions and reinsurance.
Regulation varies by country, so check current rules on rating, reserves, solvency, mandated benefits and consumer protection.

en.title: General Insurance Pricing
en.short: Frequency and severity, risk classification, deductibles, limits, no-claims discounts and premium principles.

sections.heading: Frequency and severity
sections.text: Frequency is the expected number of claims per exposure unit, such as one car-year. Severity is the average cost of a claim. The pure premium is frequency × severity. For a portfolio, expected aggregate claims = exposure × frequency × severity. Frequency is often modelled with a Poisson or negative binomial count model, and severity with a skewed continuous model such as gamma or lognormal. These models are fitted to past claims, then adjusted for trends such as inflation.

sections.heading: Risk classification
sections.text: Risk classification puts policies into groups with similar expected cost using rating factors such as age, location and vehicle group. A factor is useful only if it is measurable, verifiable and statistically credible. Classification can improve fairness between groups but can be controversial. Rules on permitted factors differ by country, so check the local insurance regulator.

sections.heading: Deductibles and limits
sections.text:
Deductibles and limits change the claim cost. A deductible, also called an excess, is the amount the insured pays first. A limit is the most the insurer pays. Pricing must use the claim-size distribution, not just the average claim.

Example: 1,000 policies have frequency 0.08 and average severity 25,000. Pure premium = 0.08 × 25,000 = 2,000 per policy. If every claim exceeds a 5,000 deductible, severity falls to 20,000 and pure premium to 0.08 × 20,000 = 1,600. Claims below the deductible would reduce frequency too.

sections.heading: Discounts and premium principles
sections.text: A no-claims discount (NCD) lowers the premium after claim-free years. It rewards safe drivers and discourages small claims, but it must be modelled with discount levels and claim transitions. Premium principles set the loading above expected claims. The expected value principle uses expected claims plus a loading. The variance and standard deviation principles add a risk load based on variability. Gross premium must also cover expenses, profit and capital, and meet solvency rules.

keyPoints: Pure premium = frequency × severity.
Expected aggregate claims = exposure × frequency × severity.
A deductible makes the insured pay first; a limit caps the insurer’s payment.
Risk classification groups similar risks using measurable, credible rating factors.
A no-claims discount is a transition system that rewards claim-free years.
Premium principles add loadings: expected value uses expected claims plus a loading, variance uses expected claims plus a multiple of variance.

en.title: General Insurance Reserving
en.short: Claims triangles, chain ladder, Bornhuetter-Ferguson, IBNR, run-off and reserve uncertainty.

sections.heading: Claims triangles and IBNR
sections.text:
A claims triangle shows cumulative paid or incurred claims by origin period, often accident year, and development period. Each row follows one origin year as it matures; later cells are missing. The pattern of development helps estimate claims still to come.

The incurred but not reported (IBNR) reserve covers claims incurred but not yet recorded, plus expected development on reported claims. Some actuaries separate IBNR from IBNER, incurred but not enough reported. The reserve is an estimate, not a known debt.

sections.heading: Chain ladder
sections.text:
The chain ladder method estimates development factors from the triangle. A factor is cumulative claims at a later development period divided by the previous figure, usually summed across origin years. Example in millions, using incurred claims:

Origin 2021: 100, 150
Origin 2022: 120, ?

Factor 0 to 1 = 150 ÷ 100 = 1.5.
Ultimate for 2022 = 120 × 1.5 = 180.
IBNR = 180 − 120 = 60.

The method assumes past development continues. It is simple but sensitive to outliers and changes in claims handling.

sections.heading: Bornhuetter-Ferguson
sections.text:
Bornhuetter-Ferguson (BF) blends the chain ladder with a prior expectation, often from pricing. It uses the expected proportion still unreported from the triangle.

BF ultimate = reported claims + (1 − proportion developed) × prior expected ultimate.

For a year with 120 reported, 60% developed and prior expected ultimate 250:
BF ultimate = 120 + (1 − 0.60) × 250 = 120 + 100 = 220.
IBNR = 220 − 120 = 100.

BF is steadier than chain ladder for immature years, but it depends on the prior.

sections.heading: Run-off and uncertainty
sections.text: Run-off is the period after cover stops or a portfolio closes, when outstanding claims are settled. Reserves are released as claims are paid. Reserve uncertainty comes from unknown claim counts, settlement delays, inflation, court awards and model error. Actuaries test sensitivity, compare methods and may use stochastic models to estimate a range. Rules differ by country, so check the local regulator and actuarial standards.

keyPoints: A claims triangle shows cumulative claims by origin and development period.
Chain ladder development factor = later cumulative claims ÷ earlier cumulative claims, usually summed across origins.
Chain ladder ultimate = latest cumulative claims × product of future development factors.
IBNR reserve = estimated ultimate − reported (incurred) claims to date; ultimate minus paid gives total unpaid claims, which also includes case reserves.
Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate = reported claims + (1 − proportion developed) × prior expected ultimate.
Run-off settles outstanding claims after cover stops; reserve uncertainty is tested by sensitivity and stochastic methods.

en.title: Risk Theory and Credibility
en.short: Aggregate claims, compound distributions, ruin probability and credibility-weighted experience rating.

sections.heading: Collective risk model
sections.text: The collective risk model treats aggregate claims S as a random sum S = X1 + ... + XN. N is the random number of claims in a period; each Xi is an individual claim amount. The Xi are independent of N and usually independent and identically distributed (iid). The model describes a portfolio, not one policy, and gives the distribution needed for pricing and capital.

sections.heading: Compound distributions
sections.text: If N is random and the Xi are iid, S has a compound distribution. When N is Poisson with mean λ, S is compound Poisson. Then E[S] = E[N]E[X] and Var(S) = E[N]Var(X) + Var(N)(E[X])². For Poisson N, Var(S) = λE[X²]. Example: λ = 4, mean claim = 500, claim variance = 250,000. E[S] = 4 × 500 = 2,000. Var(S) = 4 × (250,000 + 500²) = 4 × 500,000 = 2,000,000. The standard deviation is √2,000,000 ≈ 1,414.

sections.heading: Ruin theory
sections.text: Ruin theory studies the surplus U(t) = u + ct − S(t), where u is initial surplus, c is premium income per unit time and S(t) is aggregate claims up to t. Ruin occurs if U(t) falls below zero; ψ(u) is the probability of ruin from initial surplus u. In the classical Poisson model, c = (1 + θ)λμ, where θ > 0 is the safety loading and μ is mean claim size. The adjustment coefficient R solves λ + cR = λE[e^{RX}], and Lundberg’s inequality gives ψ(u) ≤ e^{−Ru}. Larger u and θ usually reduce ψ(u).

sections.heading: Credibility and experience rating
sections.text: Credibility theory blends an individual risk’s own experience with collateral data: premium = Z × individual estimate + (1 − Z) × collective estimate. Z is the credibility factor, between 0 and 1. In Bühlmann credibility, Z = n/(n + K), with K = v/a, where v is expected process variance and a is variance of the risk means. Experience rating applies this to past claims, so more observations, or more variation between risks, raise Z.

keyPoints: Aggregate claims are S = X1 + ... + XN, with N random and Xi iid and independent of N.
E[S] = E[N]E[X] and Var(S) = E[N]Var(X) + Var(N)(E[X])²; for Poisson N, Var(S) = λE[X²].
Ruin probability ψ(u) is the chance surplus U(t) = u + ct − S(t) ever falls below zero.
In the classical model c = (1 + θ)λμ, and Lundberg’s inequality gives ψ(u) ≤ e^{−Ru} for the adjustment coefficient R.
Credibility premium = Z × individual estimate + (1 − Z) × collective estimate, with 0 ≤ Z ≤ 1.
In Bühlmann credibility Z = n/(n + K) and K = v/a, where v is expected process variance and a is between-risk variance.

en.title: Stochastic Processes for Actuaries
en.short: Markov chains, Poisson processes and Brownian motion, with insurance and finance uses.

sections.heading: Random processes over time
sections.text: A stochastic process is a family of random variables indexed by time. The index may be discrete, as in yearly states, or continuous. A Markov chain has a finite or countable state space and the Markov property: the future depends on the present state, not on the past. Its one-step transition probabilities form a matrix P whose rows sum to 1. A Poisson process counts events that occur singly, with independent increments and a constant rate lambda. Standard Brownian motion B(t) has continuous paths, independent normal increments, B(0)=0 and Var(B(t)−B(s))=t−s. These three models are building blocks, not rivals.

sections.heading: Markov chains in insurance
sections.text: Markov chains model movement between states. In insurance, states might be no claim and claim, or current and lapsed. Suppose a policyholder is in state N (no claim) or C (claim), with P = [[0.8, 0.2], [0.3, 0.7]]. From N, the chance of staying in N for two years is 0.8×0.8 + 0.2×0.3 = 0.70. The chance of being in C is 0.30. The row sums check: 0.70+0.30=1. Actuaries use such chains for no-claims discounts, credit migration and multi-state life models. A state is absorbing if once entered it cannot be left.

sections.heading: Poisson claim counts
sections.text: A Poisson process counts claims or arrivals. If claims arrive at rate lambda = 4 per month, then in half a month the expected count is lambda t = 4×0.5 = 2. The count is Poisson with mean and variance 2. The probability of exactly two claims is P(N(0.5)=2) = e^(−2) × 2² ÷ 2! ≈ 0.2707. Waiting times between claims are exponential with mean 1 ÷ lambda = 0.25 month. General insurers use Poisson models for claim frequency; risk theory uses them in surplus and ruin models.

sections.heading: Brownian motion in finance
sections.text: Brownian motion drives continuous-time finance. Geometric Brownian motion, dS = μS dt + σS dB, gives positive asset prices with normal log returns. It underlies Black-Scholes option pricing and diffusion approximations for surplus.

keyPoints: A Markov chain has the Markov property: the future depends only on the present state.
Transition matrix rows sum to 1, and two-step probabilities are entries of P².
For a Poisson process with rate lambda, N(t) has mean and variance lambda t.
Waiting times between Poisson events are exponential with mean 1 ÷ lambda.
Standard Brownian motion has independent normal increments with variance t − s.
Geometric Brownian motion dS = μS dt + σS dB is used for asset prices and option pricing.

en.title: Statistical Modelling and Regression for Actuaries
en.short: Linear regression, generalised linear models, survival regression and time series for actuarial work.

sections.heading: Linear regression
sections.text:
Linear regression models a numeric response y as y = β0 + β1x1 + ... + βkxk + ε. The errors ε are independent with mean zero and constant variance. Ordinary least squares (OLS) minimises the sum of squared errors. Residuals are actual minus fitted. Check assumptions.

Example: for (x, y) = (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), mean x is 2 and mean y is 11/3 = 3.667. Slope = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) ÷ Σ(x−x̄)² = (1.667 + 0 + 1.333) ÷ 2 = 1.5. Intercept = 3.667 − 1.5×2 = 0.667. Prediction at x = 4 is 0.667 + 1.5×4 = 6.667.

sections.heading: Generalised linear models
sections.text: A generalised linear model (GLM) extends regression to non-normal responses, such as claim counts (Poisson) or amounts (gamma). It has a distribution, a linear predictor η = β0 + β1x1 + ... + βkxk, and a link function g with g(μ) = η, where μ is the mean response. A log link gives multiplicative effects; a logit link models a probability. Coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood. In a Poisson GLM with log link, exp(β1) is the multiplicative change in expected count for a one-unit rise in x1.

sections.heading: Survival regression
sections.text: Survival regression models time to an event, such as death or claim, when some times are censored, meaning the event is not observed for some subjects during the observation period. The Cox proportional hazards model is h(t|x) = h0(t) exp(β1x1 + ... + βkxk). h0(t) is the baseline hazard and exp(βj) is a hazard ratio: above 1 means higher hazard. Cox is semi-parametric. Accelerated failure time models assume covariates multiply survival time. Actuaries use these for mortality and lapse.

sections.heading: Time series
sections.text: Time series methods model observations ordered in time. Stationarity means the mean and variance do not change with time. Autocorrelation measures dependence between values at different lags. ARIMA models combine autoregression, differencing and moving averages; differencing removes trend. Forecasts carry uncertainty. Actuaries use time series for claims, expenses and mortality improvement, but structural breaks and short histories limit reliability.

keyPoints: OLS estimates β by minimising Σ(y − ŷ)².
A GLM links the mean μ to a linear predictor through g(μ) = β0 + β1x1 + ... + βkxk.
In a Poisson GLM with log link, exp(β1) is a multiplicative rate ratio.
The Cox model is h(t|x) = h0(t)exp(β1x1 + ... + βkxk), and exp(βj) is a hazard ratio.
ARIMA models require stationarity, often after differencing.
Always check assumptions and report estimate or forecast uncertainty.

en.title: Financial Economics for Actuaries
en.short: Covers utility, portfolio choice, CAPM, market efficiency, yield curves and asset return models.

sections.heading: Utility and risk
sections.text: Utility measures satisfaction; utility theory describes choices under uncertainty. Expected utility is Σ p_i U(W_i): the probability-weighted average of utility from each possible wealth W_i. A risk-averse person has a concave utility function, so a sure amount is preferred to a gamble with the same expected value. The certainty equivalent is the sure amount with equal utility. Risk premium is expected wealth minus certainty equivalent. Insurance and diversification suit risk-averse people.

sections.heading: Portfolio choice
sections.text:
Mean-variance portfolio choice uses expected return and variance. For two assets with weights w and 1−w, expected return is wE(R_A)+(1−w)E(R_B). Variance is w²σ_A²+(1−w)²σ_B²+2w(1−w)ρσ_Aσ_B. Diversification lowers risk when correlation ρ is below one. The efficient frontier shows portfolios with the highest expected return for each risk level. A risk-free asset gives the capital market line.

Example: A has E(R)=10%, σ=20%; B has 6%, 10%; ρ=0.5; equal weights. Portfolio return = 8%. Variance = 0.25×0.04 + 0.25×0.01 + 2×0.5×0.5×0.5×0.2×0.1 = 0.0175. Standard deviation = √0.0175 = 13.2%.

sections.heading: CAPM and efficiency
sections.text: The capital asset pricing model (CAPM) prices systematic risk. Beta measures how much an asset moves with the market. The security market line is E(R_i)=R_f+β_i[E(R_m)−R_f], where R_f is the risk-free rate and E(R_m)−R_f is the market risk premium. Unsystematic risk can be diversified away, so it earns no premium. Market efficiency means prices quickly reflect information. The weak form covers past prices, the semi-strong form public information, and the strong form all information. Tests give mixed results, so efficiency is a model, not a law.

sections.heading: Rates and returns
sections.text: The term structure is the relation between yield and maturity, shown by the yield curve. The expectations theory says long rates reflect expected future short rates. Liquidity preference adds a premium for holding longer bonds. Market segmentation says different maturities attract different investors. Asset return models include the random walk, where past returns do not predict future returns, and factor models linking returns to common factors. The lognormal model is common for prices because it keeps prices positive.

keyPoints: Expected utility is Σ p_i U(W_i), and a concave utility function indicates risk aversion.
Portfolio variance for two assets is w²σ_A²+(1−w)²σ_B²+2w(1−w)ρσ_Aσ_B.
The CAPM formula is E(R_i)=R_f+β_i[E(R_m)−R_f].
Market efficiency has weak, semi-strong and strong forms, and evidence is mixed.
The term structure relates yield to maturity, and expectations, liquidity preference and segmentation are competing explanations.
Asset return models include random walks and factor models, and the lognormal model keeps prices positive.

en.title: Derivatives and Hedging
en.short: Forwards, futures, options, binomial and Black-Scholes pricing, Greeks and hedging.

sections.heading: Forwards and futures
sections.text: A derivative’s value depends on an underlying asset, rate or index. A forward is a private contract to buy or sell at a fixed price on a future date; both sides must trade. A future is a standardised exchange-traded forward with daily settlement and margin, which is collateral. This cuts counterparty risk but adds basis risk when the hedge and exposure differ. For a non-dividend share, no-arbitrage gives F0 = S0 e^{rT}, where S0 is spot, r the risk-free rate and T time in years. If F0 is too high, borrow, buy the share and sell forward.

sections.heading: Options and pricing
sections.text:
An option gives the buyer a right, not an obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) at strike K for a premium. The one-period binomial model values it by risk-neutral probability p = (e^{rT} − d) ÷ (u − d), so C = e^{−rT}[p Cu + (1 − p) Cd]. Black-Scholes extends this to continuous trading. For a non-dividend share, C = S0 N(d1) − K e^{−rT} N(d2), with d1 = [ln(S0/K) + (r + σ²/2)T] ÷ (σ√T) and d2 = d1 − σ√T. N is the standard normal cumulative distribution function; σ volatility. Put-call parity: C + K e^{−rT} = P + S0.

Example: S0 = K = 100, r = 5%, T = 1, σ = 20%. d1 = 0.35, d2 = 0.15. With N(0.35) = 0.6368 and N(0.15) = 0.5596, C = 100(0.6368) − 100 e^{−0.05}(0.5596) = 10.45.

sections.heading: Greeks and hedging
sections.text: The Greeks measure sensitivity. Delta is the change in option value for a one-unit change in S0; for the call above delta = N(d1) = 0.6368. Gamma is the rate of change of delta, vega is sensitivity to volatility, theta to time decay and rho to interest rates. A delta-neutral hedge holds −delta units of the underlying per option, but it must be rebalanced as delta changes. This is dynamic hedging. It reduces price risk, not all risk: volatility, liquidity and model error remain.

keyPoints: A forward obliges both parties to trade at a fixed price; a future is standardised, exchange-traded and settled daily with margin.
No-arbitrage forward price for a non-dividend share is F0 = S0 e^{rT}.
A call gives the right to buy at strike K; a put gives the right to sell at strike K.
Binomial risk-neutral price: p = (e^{rT} − d) ÷ (u − d) and C = e^{−rT}[p Cu + (1 − p) Cd].
Black-Scholes call: C = S0 N(d1) − K e^{−rT} N(d2), with d1 = [ln(S0/K) + (r + σ²/2)T] ÷ (σ√T) and d2 = d1 − σ√T.
Delta = N(d1) for a call; delta hedging is dynamic and leaves volatility, liquidity and model risk.

en.title: Asset-Liability Management
en.short: Duration, convexity, immunization, matching, investment strategy and solvency rules.

sections.heading: Duration and convexity
sections.text: Asset-liability management (ALM) coordinates assets and liabilities to meet promises. Duration measures interest-rate sensitivity. Macaulay duration is the present-value-weighted average time of cash flows: D = Σ t PV(CF_t) ÷ Σ PV(CF_t). Modified duration is D ÷ (1 + y) for annual yield y. A small yield change Δy changes value by about −modified duration × Δy × value. Convexity measures the curvature of the price-yield relationship; it improves the estimate: value change ≈ −D_mod × Δy × V + ½ × convexity × (Δy)² × V. Higher convexity is safer.

sections.heading: Immunization and matching
sections.text: Cash-flow matching, or dedication, buys bonds whose payments match each liability date. It is exact but costly and inflexible. Duration immunization matches present values and durations so small parallel yield changes affect assets and liabilities similarly. It needs rebalancing as time and yields change. If asset convexity exceeds liability convexity, the surplus (assets minus liabilities) is better protected against larger moves. For uncertain cash flows, such as insurance claims, full matching is hard; models and buffers are used.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A liability of 100,000 due in five years at 5% has present value 100,000 ÷ 1.05^5 = 78,352.62 and duration 5. Modified duration = 5 ÷ 1.05 = 4.7619. If yield rises by 1%, the approximate fall is 78,352.62 × 0.047619 = 3,731.08. A matching asset portfolio with the same present value and duration would fall by about the same amount, so the surplus is immunized for a small shift. Actual prices reflect convexity.

sections.heading: Strategy and solvency
sections.text: Investment strategy starts from the liability profile: timing, amount, currency and uncertainty. It balances return, liquidity, credit risk and capital. Solvency means assets exceed liabilities with a margin; regulators set valuation and capital rules. These rules vary by country and change, so check the current official source. For example, Solvency II applies in the EU and NAICOM regulates insurers in Nigeria. ALM supports solvency by limiting mismatch risk, not removing it.

keyPoints: ALM coordinates assets and liabilities to meet promises and limit mismatch risk.
Macaulay duration D = Σ t PV(CF_t) ÷ Σ PV(CF_t), and modified duration = D ÷ (1 + y).
Approximate value change = −modified duration × Δy × value, and convexity adds ½ × convexity × (Δy)² × value.
Immunization requires equal present values and equal durations, and it must be rebalanced.
Cash-flow matching matches each liability date; duration matching protects against small parallel yield changes.
Solvency rules and capital requirements vary by country, so check the current official source.

en.title: Actuarial Modelling and Simulation
en.short: Deterministic and stochastic models, Monte Carlo simulation, validation, sensitivity and communication.

sections.heading: Deterministic and stochastic models
sections.text: A model is a simplified representation of a real system, built from assumptions, variables and parameters. A deterministic model gives one output for each input set. A stochastic model includes random variation, so outputs form a distribution. Actuaries use deterministic models for central estimates and stochastic models for risk and uncertainty. Both need clear time steps, cash-flow timing and units.

sections.heading: Monte Carlo simulation
sections.text:
Monte Carlo simulation generates many random scenarios from chosen distributions, runs the model on each, and summarises the results. It estimates means, percentiles and probabilities. More simulations reduce sampling error, but not errors in the model or its assumptions. Pseudo-random numbers are computer-generated values that behave like random draws.

Example: a fund starts with 100,000 and pays 30,000 at each year end. With a fixed return of 5% a year, the balance after three years is 100,000 × 1.05³ − 30,000 × (1.05² + 1.05 + 1) = 115,762.50 − 94,575 = 21,187.50. If 10,000 simulations give 1,200 balances below zero, the estimated probability of exhaustion is 1,200 ÷ 10,000 = 0.12, or 12%. Its standard error is √(0.12 × 0.88 ÷ 10,000) ≈ 0.0032, about 0.32 percentage points.

sections.heading: Validation and sensitivity
sections.text: Validation asks whether a model is fit for its purpose. Checks include face validity with experts, back-testing against past data, out-of-sample testing and checking limiting cases. Sensitivity analysis changes one input at a time to see which assumptions drive the output. Scenario and stress tests change several inputs together. Validation tests the model; sensitivity explains its behaviour.

sections.heading: Communicating results
sections.text: Communication should state the question, assumptions, data, method and limitations. Present a central estimate with a range or distribution, not a single number alone. Explain model risk, the risk of error from wrong assumptions or implementation. Use clear tables and plain language, and record the model version so results can be reproduced.

keyPoints: Deterministic projection: balance = starting fund × (1+r)^n − payment × Σ(1+r)^(n−k) for a payment at the end of year k; stochastic models add random variation.
Monte Carlo simulation draws many random scenarios and summarises the resulting distribution.
Monte Carlo probability estimate = number of simulated events ÷ number of simulations.
Standard error of a proportion = √(p(1−p) ÷ n).
Validation checks fitness for purpose; sensitivity analysis changes one input at a time.
Communicate assumptions, a range or distribution, model risk and limitations.

en.title: Professional Ethics, Regulation and Communication
en.short: Codes, conflicts, disclosure, peer review, regulation and clear communication for actuaries.

sections.heading: Codes and conflicts
sections.text: An actuarial code of conduct is a set of principles and rules that a professional body expects members to follow. Codes differ, but common themes are integrity, competence, care, confidentiality and not misleading anyone. A conflict of interest arises when a personal interest, such as a shareholding or a family link, could bias professional judgement. The actuary should identify it early, disclose it in writing, and avoid the work or manage it so that advice stays independent.

sections.heading: Disclosure and peer review
sections.text: Disclosure means giving the people who rely on the work the facts they need to judge it. That includes assumptions, data limits, methods and any interest that might affect objectivity. Peer review is a check by another qualified actuary who was not involved in the work. It tests whether the method, assumptions and calculations are reasonable. It supports quality, but it does not remove the original actuary’s responsibility.

sections.heading: Regulation varies
sections.text: Actuarial regulation varies by country. In some places the professional body sets the code, qualifications and disciplinary process. In others, financial regulators also impose statutory duties, such as an appointed actuary who reports on an insurer’s financial condition. The UK’s Institute and Faculty of Actuaries and the US Society of Actuaries are examples of professional bodies. Reserved titles, continuing education and signing roles differ, so check the current official rules for the country where you work.

sections.heading: Communication and a case
sections.text: Clear communication means explaining technical results in plain language. A written report should state its purpose, data, methods, assumptions, results, uncertainty and limitations. An oral briefing should focus on what the stakeholder must decide, and the actuary should check that the message was understood. In a Lagos case, Ngozi advises a life insurer on reserves and holds shares in a reinsurer seeking its business. She discloses the holding, sells the shares or declines the work, and has her report peer reviewed before the board sees it.

keyPoints: An actuarial code of conduct sets principles such as integrity, competence, confidentiality and not misleading.
A conflict of interest must be identified, disclosed and avoided or managed.
Disclosure gives users the assumptions, limits and interests they need to judge the work.
Peer review is an independent check by another qualified actuary, not a transfer of responsibility.
Actuarial regulation and reserved roles differ by country, so check current official rules.
Clear reports and briefings explain assumptions, uncertainty and limitations in plain language.

en.title: Advanced Life Contingencies and Stochastic Mortality
en.short: Advanced life contingency models, mortality improvement, stochastic mortality and pricing under uncertainty.

sections.heading: Advanced contingency models
sections.text:
Advanced life contingency models value benefits that depend on survival or death when mortality varies by age, calendar time and duration. Select mortality depends on time since underwriting; ultimate mortality applies later. Cohort mortality follows one generation; period mortality uses one calendar year. Improvement builds up over time, so a period table without a projection can misstate long-term costs.

These models also allow continuous payment, fractional ages and joint lives. The mortality basis is no longer fixed.

sections.heading: Mortality improvement
sections.text: Mortality improvement is the fall in death rates over time. A simple projection uses a reduction factor r: q(x,t+1)=q(x,t)(1−r). After h years, q(x,t+h)=q(x,t)(1−r)^h. Choose r by age, sex and country from past data, but past improvement need not continue. Improvement lowers life insurance costs but raises annuity and pension costs, because more people survive.

sections.heading: Stochastic mortality
sections.text: Stochastic mortality treats future death rates as random. The Lee-Carter model writes ln m(x,t)=a_x+b_x k_t+ε, where a_x is the average age pattern, b_x the sensitivity to the time index k_t, and ε random error. The CBD model uses two time factors and is common at older ages. Simulate many paths to obtain distributions of annuity values, reserves and capital rather than one figure.

sections.heading: Pricing and reserving
sections.text:
Price and reserve using expected present value plus a risk margin. For a term insurance, EPV = Σ v^t × probability of death in year t × sum assured. With stochastic mortality, EPV is the mean over simulated paths; the reserve distribution informs percentiles and capital. Margins and rules differ by country, so check the local regulator.

Example: the base table has q75=0.02. With improvement r=1.5% a year for 10 years, q75 in 10 years is 0.02×(1−0.015)^10=0.02×0.85973=0.01719. For 1,000,000 payable at year end and i=5%, v=1÷1.05=0.952381. EPV at q=0.02 is 1,000,000×0.02×0.952381=19,047.62. At q=0.01719 it is 1,000,000×0.01719×0.952381=16,371.43. The difference is 2,676.19.

keyPoints: Advanced life contingency models must allow mortality to vary by age, calendar time and duration.
q(x,t+h)=q(x,t)(1−r)^h projects mortality with a constant annual reduction factor r.
The Lee-Carter model is ln m(x,t)=a_x+b_x k_t+ε.
Stochastic mortality gives distributions of annuity values, reserves and capital, not a single figure.
EPV = Σ v^t × probability of death in year t × sum assured.
Risk margins and reserving rules differ by country, so check the local regulator.

en.title: Enterprise Risk Management and Solvency
en.short: ERM frameworks, risk appetite, economic capital and country-specific solvency rules.

sections.heading: ERM and appetite
sections.text:
Enterprise risk management (ERM) is a coordinated process for identifying, assessing, managing and monitoring all risks that affect a firm’s objectives. Two common frameworks are COSO ERM and ISO 31000. They set principles and processes, not fixed capital rules. The board oversees ERM; management implements it.

Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk a board is willing to accept to meet its objectives. It is expressed through limits and tolerances. Risk capacity is the maximum risk the firm can bear before failing. Appetite should sit below capacity.

sections.heading: Economic capital
sections.text:
Economic capital is the capital a firm holds against unexpected losses over a chosen horizon and confidence level. If expected losses are paid from premiums, economic capital = Q(α) − E(L), where Q(α) is the loss quantile at confidence α and E(L) is expected loss. Value at risk (VaR) is that quantile. Expected shortfall is the average loss beyond it. This is not the same as regulatory capital.

Example in units: expected loss 40, 99.5% quantile 300. Economic capital = 300 − 40 = 260. Available capital 280 gives surplus 280 − 260 = 20. Solvency ratio = 280 ÷ 260 = 107.7%.

sections.heading: Solvency regimes
sections.text: Solvency means a firm can meet its liabilities as they fall due, with enough capital for adverse events. Regulators set minimum solvency capital, and regimes vary by country. The EU’s Solvency II sets a solvency capital requirement calibrated to a 99.5% one-year VaR. The UK uses Solvency UK; the US uses NAIC (National Association of Insurance Commissioners) risk-based capital; Switzerland uses the Swiss Solvency Test. Nigeria’s NAICOM (National Insurance Commission) sets capital rules for insurers. Some supervisors use formula-based capital; others allow internal models. Rules and figures change, so check the current official source.

keyPoints: ERM coordinates risk management across the firm; COSO and ISO 31000 are common frameworks.
Risk appetite states acceptable risk; risk capacity is the maximum bearable.
Economic capital = Q(α) − E(L) when expected losses are met from premiums.
Regulatory capital is set by the supervisor and differs by country.
Solvency ratio = available capital ÷ required capital; above 100% means surplus.
Solvency II is an EU regime calibrated to 99.5% one-year VaR; other countries use different rules.

en.title: Actuarial Data Science and Machine Learning
en.short: Covers GLMs, machine learning, validation, interpretability and ethical data use in insurance and pensions.

sections.heading: From GLMs to ML
sections.text: A generalised linear model (GLM) relates the mean of a response to a linear predictor through a link function. Logistic regression, a GLM for a yes or no outcome such as a claim, uses the logit link: log(p ÷ (1 − p)) = β0 + β1x1 + ... . Machine learning methods include decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting and neural networks. They can capture interactions and nonlinearity without a stated link, but they need more data and are harder to explain. In insurance and pensions, GLMs remain common because regulators and actuaries can audit them.

sections.heading: Validation and overfitting
