sections.text: Validation estimates performance on unseen data. Split data into training, validation and test sets, or use cross-validation. For claim models, check discrimination (how well the model ranks risk, often by the area under the ROC curve) and calibration (whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies). Overfitting means fitting noise in the training data; it shows as good training fit and poor test fit. Regularisation, such as ridge or lasso, shrinks coefficients to reduce overfitting.

sections.heading: Worked example: logistic GLM
sections.text: Take a logistic model logit(p) = −2 + 0.5x. At x = 2, logit = −2 + 1 = −1. Odds = e^−1 = 0.3679. Probability p = 0.3679 ÷ 1.3679 = 0.269, or 26.9%. At x = 3, logit = −0.5, odds = 0.6065, p = 0.6065 ÷ 1.6065 = 0.378, or 37.8%. A one-unit rise in x multiplies odds by e^0.5 = 1.65.

sections.heading: Interpretability and ethics
sections.text: Interpretability means explaining how inputs affect outputs. In a logistic GLM, coefficients give log-odds changes; odds ratios are e^β. For complex models, use SHAP values (a prediction attribution method) or a simple approximate model, and document limits. Ethical use requires a legal basis, data minimisation, security and fairness testing. Avoid proxy variables that discriminate by sex, ethnicity, disability or other protected grounds. Pricing and underwriting must be justified and comply with local law; check the current rules in the relevant country. In pensions, poor data can harm member benefits, so governance and audit trails matter.

keyPoints: A GLM links the mean response to a linear predictor through a link function; logistic regression uses log(p ÷ (1 − p)) = β0 + β1x1 + ... .
Machine learning can capture nonlinearity and interactions but is less transparent than a GLM.
Validate on unseen data and check both discrimination and calibration, not training fit alone.
Overfitting is good training fit with poor test performance; regularisation helps control it.
Odds ratio = e^β, so a one-unit rise in x multiplies odds by e^β.
Use data lawfully and fairly, test for bias and avoid proxies for protected characteristics; check local insurance rules.

en.title: Research Methods and Dissertation in Actuarial Science
en.short: Reviewing literature, designing actuarial research, cleaning data, reproducibility, inference and dissertation writing.

sections.heading: Review and design
sections.text: A literature review is a critical summary of existing research, not a list. It should state the question, explain how you searched, and identify gaps your dissertation addresses. Research design is the plan that links question to evidence. Decide whether the study is descriptive, explanatory or predictive, and whether data are primary or secondary. Define the population, the sampling frame (the list you sample from) and the sampling method. In actuarial work, common designs use policy records, claims data, surveys or published tables. State inclusion criteria and limitations early, because they shape what you can infer.

sections.heading: Data and reproducibility
sections.text:
Data collection must follow the design. Record sources, dates, definitions and units. Data cleaning removes errors, duplicates and impossible values, and handles missing data. Keep a log of every change. Reproducibility means another researcher can rerun your analysis and obtain the same results. Save raw data unchanged, write scripts rather than manual edits, and record software versions and random seeds.

Worked example: a claims file has 1,000 rows. You find 60 rows with missing claim amounts and 10 duplicate policy records, with no overlap. After removing both, 1,000 − 60 − 10 = 930 rows remain. Report this flow in the dissertation.

sections.heading: Inference and writing
sections.text: Statistical inference uses sample data to draw conclusions about a wider population. Report estimates with uncertainty, such as confidence intervals, and state assumptions. Avoid causal language unless the design supports it. A dissertation usually has an abstract, introduction, literature review, methods, results, discussion and conclusion. Write for an examiner who is an actuary but not a specialist in your exact topic. Define terms, label tables, and explain every figure. Keep an audit trail so your claims can be checked.

keyPoints: A literature review identifies a gap, not just summarises sources.
Research design links the research question to evidence and limitations.
Rows after cleaning = starting rows − missing rows − duplicate rows.
Reproducibility requires raw data, scripts, software versions and random seeds.
Report estimates with confidence intervals and state assumptions.
A dissertation needs a clear structure and an audit trail.
